I confused “barato” with “caro” and instead was the a**hole in a navy sweatsuit unknowingly ordering Johnny blue. I drank my vastly overpriced, misanthropic whiskey in self-disgusted silence while my friends danced to songs exactly like this. I never returned to the clubs, there or anywhere else—except for an ill-fated tryst in Vieques years later where I split my pants—but you bet your culata I made lifelong friends in that little foosball bar. One of her best known songs as well as the most controversial record of her career. It's about the freedom a woman receives from birth control pills. The song tells a story of a wife who is upset about her husband getting her pregnant year after year, but is now happy bc she can control her own reproductive choices because she has "the pill" (which had been introduced in 1960). The song, like many of Lynn's other hits, suggested her personal life: she'd had SIX children, FOUR of whom were born BEFORE SHE WAS 20! The song's frank discussion of birth control, something that was considered risqué subject matter at the time (especially in country music), led to a number of country radio stations refusing to play it. In an interview, Lynn recounted how she had been congratulated after the song's success by a number of rural physicians, telling her how "The Pill" had done more to highlight the availability of birth control in isolated, rural areas, than all the literature they had released.

songs.title: Symphony No. 9, in D minor, Choral, Op. 125: II. Molto vivace
songs.artistText: Ludwig van Beethoven, Tbilisi Symphony Orchestra, Odysseas Dimitriadis
songs.note:
I'm sparing you with just this excerpt. Let me nerd out on you for a minute about this second movement of the 9th. It is set up in A-B-A form, and within each A section there is a separate a, b, c form, and within that substructure there is a 5-part fugue. I know you wont hear this when you listen, but trust that that is pretty nutty. Especially because...he wrote this while completely deaf (this would have been my disability prompt pick). 

There is an amazing story about the first time this symphony was performed: there were two conductors, one actually conducting, and the other is Beethoven who can't hear anything, flailing around like a madman based on where he thinks they are in the music. When it ended (the final movement is Ode to Joy btw) the crowd went crazy. A member of the orchestra had to turn Beethoven around to see the applause because he could not hear it. And that's a perfect music story. 

Now go listen to the full thing.
